title: Idiomatic C# after five years (style that scales)
hook: Idiomatic C# is not clever code — it is code other .NET engineers read without friction: async all the way for I/O, sealed by default, composition over inheritance, pattern matching over nested ifs, and names that match the Base Class Library (BCL).

blocks.text: After five years you default to: IAsyncEnumerable for streaming, records for immutable DTOs, early returns, guard clauses, Dependency Injection constructor injection, and ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries. You avoid Hungarian notation, underscore prefixes on locals, and Java-style getters in favor of properties. You use var when the type is obvious from the right-hand side.

entries.plainDefinition: Core .NET APIs shipped with the runtime (System.*).
entries.example: List<T>, Task, Span<T> — naming follows BCL patterns.

entries.plainDefinition: Early validation that returns or throws before main logic.
Prevents further inheritance — default for classes not designed as base classes.

blocks.text: Code review at senior level is about readability and failure modes, not syntax trivia. Idiomatic services use async Redis, return Result types instead of exceptions for expected failures (module 09), and keep controllers thin. Matching Microsoft naming guidelines makes onboarding faster — critical for teams shipping microservices.

blocks.title: Read like the BCL
blocks.body: Before inventing a pattern, check how System.Text.Json or ASP.NET Core does it — that is the style bar.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Java-style GetUser/setUser instead of User property. public fields on DTOs. God classes with 2000 lines. Blocking async (.Result) in ASP.NET handlers.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: idiomatic claims need measurement — run BenchmarkDotNet on the hot path before switching to ValueTask, stackalloc, or record struct rows. A baseline MethodImpl + MemoryDiagnoser run comparing string.Split versus span walk on a CSV fixture gives numbers for code review. dotnet-counters gen-0 on staging after adopting IAsyncEnumerable paging validates that idiomatic streaming actually reduced allocations.

snippet.label: BenchmarkDotNet — prove idiomatic span parse wins
snippet.explanation: MemoryDiagnoser shows gen-0 delta between Split (allocates string[]) and span walk — idiomatic choice backed by data, not preference.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming ValueTask or span is faster without BenchmarkDotNet numbers. Sync I/O inside async-named methods. Deep inheritance instead of sealed service + interfaces. Clever one-liners that hide failure modes. Not reading BCL patterns before inventing your own container.

interviewTakeaways: Idiomatic C# = async I/O, sealed services, records, switch expressions, guard clauses — match BCL style.
Performance idioms (span, ValueTask, record struct) require BenchmarkDotNet or dotnet-counters proof.
In production, MemoryDiagnoser on Split vs span parse quantifies gen-0 before approving hot-path refactors.
60s: Read like BCL. async for I/O. sealed default. patterns over nested if. BenchmarkDotNet before micro-optimizations. Guard clauses early return.
Follow-up: when is ConfigureAwait(false) idiomatic in library code?
commonPitfalls: Claiming span/ValueTask is faster without BenchmarkDotNet gets you rejected — measure first.
Sync I/O in async-named methods — blocks thread pool under load.
Strong answer: 'Idiomatic is readable BCL-style code. Perf idioms need MemoryDiagnoser proof. IAsyncEnumerable for streaming. Result for expected misses.'
